# Fuzzy RD Designs {#sec-rd}

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, cache = TRUE)
```

Some instruments come from a rule with a cutoff. A program is mandatory above a population threshold, or a polling station is added each time registered voters exceed a cap. Such a design is a fuzzy regression discontinuity (RD) design, and only the jump at the cutoff is as good as random. A treatment "predicted" from the rule also varies smoothly with the running variable, the variable behind the rule. Because this smooth variation may affect the outcome directly, it can make the first stage look much stronger than the jump alone.

To specify a fuzzy RD design in `ivDiag`, use `running` and `cutoff`. The instrument is the indicator for crossing the cutoff. The controls include a polynomial in the distance to the cutoff, fitted separately on each side, so that only the jump identifies the effect. Set the polynomial order with `rd.poly` (1 by default).

To restrict the sample to units within a given distance of the cutoff, use `bandwidth`. These units receive triangular kernel weights by default. For equal weights, set `kernel = "uniform"`. Without a bandwidth, the whole sample receives equal weights, and `rd$kernel` reports `"uniform"`. With several cutoffs, each unit is compared with its nearest cutoff, and cutoff fixed effects are added.

## A simulated example

In the simulated example below, take-up rises smoothly with the running variable and jumps at zero. The "predicted" treatment follows both.
```{r rd_sim}
library(ivDiag)
set.seed(2)
n <- 2000
x <- runif(n, -1, 1)
u <- rnorm(n)
d <- as.numeric(0.2 + 0.6 * x + 0.3 * (x >= 0) + 0.3 * u + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3) > 0.5)
y <- 2 * d + 1.5 * x - x^2 + u
p_hat <- 0.2 + 0.6 * x + 0.3 * (x >= 0)  # treatment predicted from the rule
rd <- data.frame(y = y, d = d, x = x, p_hat = p_hat)
```

@fig-rd-sim shows the share treated in narrow bins of `x`, with a straight line fitted on each side of the cutoff. Take-up rises with `x` on both sides. The gap between the two lines at zero is the jump that a fuzzy RD uses.
```{r}
#| label: fig-rd-sim
#| fig-cap: "Share treated by the running variable, simulated data"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
bins <- cut(x, seq(-1, 1, by = 0.1))
mid <- seq(-0.95, 0.95, by = 0.1)
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(mid, tapply(d, bins, mean), pch = 19, col = "#004a8c", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Running variable (x)", ylab = "Share treated (d)", las = 1)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
for (side in list(x < 0, x >= 0)) {
  fit <- lm(d ~ x, subset = side)
  xs <- range(x[side])
  lines(xs, predict(fit, data.frame(x = xs)), col = "#004a8c")
}
```

We estimate the effect twice: with the predicted treatment as the instrument, and as a fuzzy RD.
```{r rd_sim_est}
# predicted treatment as the instrument, running variable ignored
g0 <- ivDiag(data = rd, Y = "y", D = "d", Z = "p_hat", bootstrap = FALSE)
# fuzzy RD: crossing the cutoff, linear in x on each side
g1 <- ivDiag(data = rd, Y = "y", D = "d", running = "x", cutoff = 0,
             bootstrap = FALSE)
rbind(predicted = c(g0$est_2sls[1, 1:2], F.effective = g0$F_stat[["F.effective"]]),
      fuzzy_RD = c(g1$est_2sls[1, 1:2], F.effective = g1$F_stat[["F.effective"]]))
g1$rd
```

The predicted-treatment instrument reports a far stronger first stage and a biased estimate (the true effect is 2). This occurs because it also uses the smooth relationship between `x` and both `d` and `y`. The fuzzy RD uses only the jump at the cutoff. Its instrument is weaker but valid, and its AR set and the *tF* procedure account for that weakness [@feir2016weak].

## Polling station size and vote buying

@rueda2017 asks whether smaller polling stations make vote buying easier to enforce in Colombia, since brokers can check the published results of small groups of voters. By law, a polling station may serve at most a fixed number of registered voters: 400 in 2006 and 2007, 500 in 2010, and 350 in 2011. Each time a municipality's registered voters cross a multiple of this cap, one more station opens. The rule therefore predicts a drop in the average station size. The study uses the predicted size as the instrument for the actual size.

| Summary | |
|----------------|-----------------------|
| Unit of analysis | municipality in one election |
| Treatment | average polling station size, in logs (`lm_pob_mesa`) |
| Instrument | average size predicted by the rule, in logs (`lz_pob_mesa_f`) |
| Outcome | incidence of vote buying (`e_vote_buying`) |
| Controls | log population, log registered voters |

The `rueda` data do not record the election year, so we recover the cap. Most municipalities appear in all four elections, and their rows are in election order, so the row gives the year and the cap. The rule confirms this order: in every row where only one cap reproduces the predicted size (registered voters divided by the number of stations the rule requires), that cap is the one for the row's year. For the other municipalities, we take the cap whose rule reproduces the predicted size. We then measure registered voters in units of the cap (`ratio`). A new station opens each time `ratio` crosses an integer, so every integer is a cutoff.
```{r rueda_ratio}
voters <- exp(rueda$lpotencial)  # registered voters
caps <- c(350, 400, 500)
err <- sapply(caps, function(cap) abs(log(voters / ceiling(voters / cap)) - rueda$lz_pob_mesa_f))
cap_rule <- caps[apply(err, 1, which.min)]  # the cap whose rule reproduces the predicted size
# municipalities in all four elections: rows are in election order (2006, 2007, 2010, 2011)
pos <- ave(seq_along(voters), rueda$muni_code, FUN = seq_along)
n_obs <- ave(seq_along(voters), rueda$muni_code, FUN = length)
rueda$cap <- ifelse(n_obs == 4, c(400, 400, 500, 350)[pos], cap_rule)
rueda$ratio <- voters / rueda$cap
table(rueda$cap)
quantile(rueda$ratio, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))
```

@fig-rueda plots each municipality-election with `ratio` below 10.5 (no municipality has fewer than `r round(min(rueda$ratio), 2)` times the cap). The vertical axis shows the actual average station size as a share of the cap, and the line shows the size predicted by the rule. Between two cutoffs, the predicted size rises steadily with registered voters. At each cutoff, it drops. These drops shrink as `ratio` grows: crossing 2, the predicted size falls from the cap to 2/3 of it, but crossing 10, only to 10/11 of it. Many municipalities have one or two more stations than the rule requires, forming lower copies of the saw-tooth pattern, so their size does not follow the rule's drops.
```{r}
#| label: fig-rueda
#| fig-cap: "Polling station size and the rule near the first cutoffs, Rueda (2017)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: "95%"
near <- subset(rueda, ratio < 10.5)
grid <- seq(1.3, 10.5, by = 0.001)
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 2.5, 1))
plot(near$ratio, exp(near$lm_pob_mesa) / near$cap, pch = 1, cex = 0.5,
     col = adjustcolor("#004a8c", 0.5), xlim = c(1.3, 10.5), las = 1,
     xlab = "Registered voters / cap", ylab = "Average station size / cap")
lines(grid, grid / ceiling(grid), col = "gray30")
legend("top", inset = c(0, -0.1), xpd = TRUE, horiz = TRUE, bty = "n",
       legend = c("Municipality-election", "Predicted by the rule"),
       pch = c(1, NA), lty = c(NA, 1), col = c("#004a8c", "gray30"))
```

To specify the fuzzy RD, pass `ratio` as the running variable and the integers as cutoffs. `ivDiag` then compares each municipality with its nearest cutoff and adds cutoff fixed effects. Below, we fit the first stage twice: with the predicted size as the instrument, as in the study, and as a fuzzy RD. We report only the first-stage *F* statistics.
```{r rueda_spec}
# predicted size as the instrument, running variable ignored
f_pred <- ivDiag(data = rueda, Y = "e_vote_buying", D = "lm_pob_mesa",
                 Z = "lz_pob_mesa_f", controls = c("lpopulation", "lpotencial"),
                 cl = "muni_code", bootstrap = FALSE, run.AR = FALSE)
# fuzzy RD: crossing a cutoff, linear in ratio on each side, cutoff fixed effects
f_rd <- ivDiag(data = rueda, Y = "e_vote_buying", D = "lm_pob_mesa",
               controls = c("lpopulation", "lpotencial"), cl = "muni_code",
               running = "ratio", cutoff = 1:ceiling(max(rueda$ratio)),
               bootstrap = FALSE, run.AR = FALSE)
rbind(predicted = f_pred$F_stat, fuzzy_RD = f_rd$F_stat)
```

With the predicted size as the instrument, the effective *F* statistic is `r format(round(f_pred$F_stat[["F.effective"]]), big.mark = ",")`, far above any conventional threshold. This number overstates the strength of the design. Between two cutoffs, the predicted size rises smoothly with registered voters (@fig-rueda), and this smooth variation drives most of the first stage. In the fuzzy RD, only the drops at the cutoffs identify the effect, and the effective *F* statistic falls to `r round(f_rd$F_stat[["F.effective"]], 2)`. The drops are small beyond the first few cutoffs, and many municipalities do not follow them. With a first stage this weak, rely on the AR set rather than the *t*-test [@feir2016weak].
